findings.issue: This is new in the delta. precheck() calls amount.setScale(2, HALF_UP) on the raw @RequestParam BigDecimal before checking any range. Spring binds the parameter with new BigDecimal(text), which accepts exponent notation. A value such as amount=1e-600000000 or amount=1e600000000 makes setScale build 10^~6e8 as a BigInteger: hundreds of MB of memory and minutes of CPU on the request thread before the 409. Only an authenticated ADMIN/FINANCE user can trigger it, it can be repeated, and the WARN line that names the actor is written only after the work finishes. Availability is the only risk. No ledger write can result.
findings.fix: Before rounding, reject when amount.scale() > 4 or amount.scale() < 0, or when amount.precision() - amount.scale() > 12 (or compare amount.abs() with MAX_AMOUNT first, which is cheap). Use the same 409 and WARN path.

findings.issue: The register-amount cap is skipped when d.expected() is null, so the check fails open. No such MISSING_SALE row can be created today: the job writes expected from ledger_shipments.amount, which is NOT NULL. But ledger_discrepancies.expected is a nullable column, so a hand-inserted or future row would let any amount below 10^12 through.
findings.fix: For MISSING_SALE, refuse with 409 ('No register amount; manual procedure') when d.expected() is null.

findings.issue: When a concurrent repair loses the row lock, the call returns 200 with the winner's row. It writes no log line and no audit record, so the losing admin's attempt and the amount they entered leave no trace.
findings.fix: When locked.isEmpty(), log at INFO or WARN: 'repair of {} by {} skipped: already resolved'.

summary: All items from d811b88 are resolved at 1662edc, and the part B guard demos in evidence.md match the code. (1) The amount is rounded HALF_UP to cents first. A rounded value that is not above 0 or not below 10^12 gets 409, and so does a value above the row's register amount (d.expected()). Every refusal is an ApplicationException, so it passes through the single catch that writes the WARN 'refused for <actor>'. The tests cover 0.004, 0, -5, 10^12, 99999999999999.99 and 100.01, and check that nothing is booked. The demos show the range test and the cap test each fail when their guard is removed. (2) No bypass: the only route is POST /api/admin/ledger/discrepancies/{id}/repair under hasAnyRole('ADMIN','FINANCE'). MISSING_SALE always goes through precheck, and recordDelivered receives the rounded cents. A larger SALE is a documented manual procedure for the Owner, not an API path. (3) AuditPublisher gets REPAIR_LEDGER_DISCREPANCY / LEDGER_DISCREPANCY / id with kind, amount, registerAmount and note. The actor is taken from the SecurityContext, the publish is fail-open, and a test asserts amount 80.00 and registerAmount 100.00. The JSON is assembled from server-side values only: kind comes from a fixed set, the amounts are BigDecimals, and quotes in the note are replaced. (4) The repair takes SELECT ... WHERE id AND resolved_at IS NULL FOR UPDATE inside a TransactionTemplate. book() checks for an existing SALE first and writes 'SALE already present (amount <booked>)', and after posting it reads the booked amount back, so detail and the log never claim an amount that was not booked. (5) The order mismatch in UNMATCHED_REVERSAL becomes a 409 with a WARN, and a test plus its guard demo cover it. (6) The Feign state check stops after max-feign-errors (default 5) errors in a row, sets FEIGN_STOPPED, and skips legacy SALEs where shipment id = order id. A test shows 5 calls, then the stop. The row lock is not test-proven, and I accept that. Money integrity rests on the SALE unique key, and the concurrent-repair test proves one SALE. The read-back keeps detail truthful. Under READ COMMITTED the lock with its resolved_at IS NULL predicate also stops a second resolve from overwriting resolved_by. This lock is defence in depth on the audit trail, not the money control. The delta adds no new dependency, endpoint, secret or PII, and all SQL uses bound parameters. The new OrderEventConsumer log prints only missing/present/invalid states, never the untrusted ids. The three minors are a BigDecimal exponent CPU/memory DoS from rounding before the range check, a cap that fails open when expected is null, and a silent 200 for the repair that loses the lock. None blocks approval.
